extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of classical geometry; readers studying Archimedes' On Conoids and Spheroids
extracted.subtask_description: Study and reproduce classical geometrical propositions about conoids and spheroids (sections by planes, tangent-plane properties, volume relations of segments) including constructions and proofs following Archimedes' methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 9 — cylinder through ellipse
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an ellipse, a plane through one of its axes and perpendicular to that of the ellipse, and a straight line OC from the centre C in the given plane (through the axis but not perpendicular to it), it is possible to find a cylinder with axis OC whose surface passes through the circumference of the given ellipse (i.e., the ellipse is a section of such a cylinder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: Draw AD and A'E parallel to CO, let DE be the line through O perpendicular to AD and A'E. Consider three cases where the other axis BB' is equal to, greater than, or less than DE. In each case construct a circle on an appropriate diameter (DE, DE' or DE with an auxiliary point K and point R) in a plane perpendicular to OC and describe a cylinder with axis OC through that circle. Proof uses perpendiculars from an arbitrary point P on the ellipse, parallels to CO, and the circle-property PN^2 = DM·ME (or equal QM), deducing PQ is parallel to CO so PQ is a generator of the cylinder and P lies on the cylinder. The text gives complete casework with the parallel/perpendicular constructions and triangle similarity arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 10 — ratio of cones and frusta
rubrics_metrics.description: Any two cones have to one another the ratio compounded of the ratios of their bases and of their heights; similarly any segments of cones compare by the compounded ratio of bases and heights. Also, any frustum of a cylinder is triple of the conical segment with same base and equal height (and a cylinder is triple of the cone with same base and height).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from Euclid references (Euc. xII.11,14) and the method of using base and height ratios. Use these compounded ratios when comparing cones, segments of cones, cylinders and frusta; the classical triple relationship between cylinder and cone is invoked for volume comparisons in later proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 11 — plane sections of conoids and spheroids
rubrics_metrics.description: Describes the types of plane sections for paraboloids, hyperboloids, and spheroids of revolution: (1) Paraboloid: plane through or parallel to axis gives a parabola equal to the generating parabola; plane at right angles to axis gives a circle. (2) Hyperboloid: plane through axis/parallel/through centre gives hyperbola (equal/similar/not similar respectively); plane at right angles to axis gives a circle. (3) Spheroid: plane through or parallel to axis gives an ellipse (equal/similar respectively); plane at right angles gives a circle. Also: if a perpendicular is drawn from any point on the surface (not on the section) to the plane of the section, that perpendicular falls within the section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are reductions to plane conic properties: intersecting the solid by planes through the axis produces plane conics whose axes are intersections of relevant planes. The statements are declared evident and used as foundational facts for subsequent propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 12 — oblique section of paraboloid is ellipse
rubrics_metrics.description: If a paraboloid of revolution is cut by a plane neither parallel nor perpendicular to the axis, and if the plane through the axis perpendicular to the cutting plane meets it in a straight line whose portion inside the paraboloid is RR', then the section is an ellipse with major axis RR' and minor axis equal to the perpendicular distance between the lines through R, R' parallel to the axis of the paraboloid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set the cutting plane perpendicular to paper and take the plane through the axis intersecting the cutting plane in RR'. For any point Q on the section draw QM perpendicular to RR' (perpendicular to paper); through M draw DMFE perpendicular to axis meeting the parabola in D,E. Show QM^2 = DM·ME (circle property) and use tangent properties (compare ratios like DM·ME : RM·MR' = AO^2 : OT^2) and similar triangles to obtain QM^2 : RM·MR' = H^2 : RR' and conclude ellipse with stated axes. Proof relies on reducing to circular sections and properties of the parabola/tangent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 13–14 — oblique sections of hyperboloid or oblong spheroid are ellipses (major axis RR')
rubrics_metrics.description: If a hyperboloid of revolution is cut by a plane meeting all generators of the enveloping cone, or an oblong spheroid is cut by a plane not perpendicular to the axis, and if a plane through the axis intersects the cutting plane at right angles in a line on which the solid intercepts RR', then the section by the cutting plane is an ellipse whose major axis is RR'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to the plane of the paper where the section is a hyperbola or ellipse with transverse/major axis AF. For a point Q on the section, draw QM perpendicular to RR' and construct circular section via DMFE perpendicular to the axis. Use QM^2 = DM·ME and tangent properties (QM^2 : RM·MR' = OA^2 : OP^2) together with comparisons OA < OP (or suitable inequalities in ellipse case) to deduce the locus is an ellipse with major axis RR'. Corollaries: for flat spheroids RR' may be the minor axis; parallel sections are similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 15 — straight lines from surface parallel to axis fall outside/in
rubrics_metrics.description: If from any point on the surface of a conoid a line be drawn parallel to the axis (paraboloid) or parallel to any line through the vertex of the enveloping cone (hyperboloid), the part of the straight line in the direction of convexity falls outside the surface, and the part in the other direction falls within it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a plane through the axis and the given point (paraboloid) or through the point and the given straight line through cone vertex (hyperboloid), reduce to corresponding plane conic where the property follows from plane conic geometry. This proposition is used to reason about where perpendiculars and parallels meet the surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 15 (2) — uniqueness and orthogonality of tangent plane
rubrics_metrics.description: If a plane touches a conoid without cutting it, it touches at one point only; and the plane through the point of contact and the axis of the conoid is at right angles to the tangent plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: if a plane touched in two points then the line joining them would lie within the conoid yet be in the tangent plane, impossible. For orthogonality, examine case at vertex and reduce general case by drawing plane through axis and the contact point, forming a circular section and showing its tangent is perpendicular to the tangent plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 16 (1) — tangent plane to spheroid touches at one point and axis-plane is orthogonal
rubrics_metrics.description: If a plane touches any of the spheroidal figures without cutting it, it touches at a single point only, and the plane through that point and the axis is at right angles to the tangent plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same method as for conoids: reduce to plane conic properties and to circular sections to show uniqueness and orthogonality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 16 (2) — erecting plane at right angles to section tangent touches solid
rubrics_metrics.description: If a conoid or spheroid is cut by a plane through the axis, and if through any tangent to the resulting conic a plane be erected at right angles to the plane of section, the erected plane will touch the conoid or spheroid in the same point where the line touches the conic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: such an erected plane cannot meet the surface at any other point because a perpendicular from any other point would be perpendicular to the tangent and fall outside the surface, contradicting the known property that perpendiculars from surface points fall within the section (Prop. 11(4)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 16 (3) — parallel tangent planes contact line passes through centre
rubrics_metrics.description: If two parallel planes touch any spheroidal figure, the line joining the points of contact passes through the centre of the spheroid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If tangent planes are perpendicular to the axis then obvious; otherwise consider plane through axis and one contact point, which is perpendicular to tangent plane and hence passes through the second contact point; both contact points then lie on a plane through axis and the line joining them passes through the centre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 17 — lines parallel to chord of contact fall outside spheroid
rubrics_metrics.description: If two parallel planes touch a spheroidal figure and another plane is drawn parallel to the tangent planes and passing through the centre, then the line drawn through any point of the resulting section's circumference parallel to the chord of contact of the tangent planes will fall outside the spheroid (in the direction of smaller segment) and within it in the other direction; if the plane through the centre is used it falls outside in the described manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by reduction to a plane proposition (plane geometry of conics). The proposition clarifies the relative position of chords and parallel lines with respect to the spheroid's convexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 18 — central plane bisects spheroid (surface & volume)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any spheroidal figure cut by a plane through the centre is divided, both in surface and in volume, into two equal parts by that plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes' proof: take another equal and similar spheroid, divide similarly, and use the method of application (classical equivalence/area/volume argument) to conclude equality of halves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 19–20 — inscribe/circumscribe segments by cylinders/frusta
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a segment cut off by a plane from a paraboloid or hyperboloid of revolution, or a spheroidal segment less than half, it is possible to inscribe in the segment a solid and circumscribe another solid each made of cylinders or frusta of cylinders of equal height such that their volume difference is less than any given solid (i.e., arbitrary close approximation by such sums).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: choose plane base perpendicular to paper, reduce to plane conic BAC, find tangent HF parallel to base, touch the solid at A and take AD as axis; construct cylinder/frustum with axis AD passing through circular or elliptical base (Prop.9). Divide cylinder/frustum into many equal-height parts and produce corresponding inscribed/circumscribed stacks of cylinders/frusta derived from the intersections with the solid; compare volumes termwise using proportions, and show the difference can be made arbitrarily small by sufficient subdivision. This sets up method of exhaustion approximating volumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 21–22 — paraboloid segment volume equalities (segment = 3 × cone/2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any segment of a paraboloid of revolution is half as large again as (i.e., 3/2 times) the cone or conical segment with the same base and axis. (Uses that cone X equal to 3 × (cone or segment of cone ABC) leads to segment equal to X.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set base perpendicular to paper and reduce to parabolic section BAC with tangent HF parallel to base touching at A. Construct corresponding cylinder/frustum and cone; using the approximating inscribed/circumscribed stacks of cylinders/frusta (Prop. 19) and comparisons of corresponding parts via proportionality and a lemma on arithmetic progressions, derive contradictions if segment were larger or smaller than the stated cone ratio; conclude equality. The proof uses termwise ratios of cylinders/frusta and the lemma BD+HO+... > 2(TO+SN+...) to compare sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 23 — equality of paraboloid segments with equal axes
rubrics_metrics.description: If from a paraboloid of revolution two segments are cut off (one by a plane perpendicular to the axis, the other by a plane not perpendicular) and if their axes are equal, then the segments are equal in volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take the plane through axis making parabolic section and show corresponding planar parabolic segments have equal triangles ABB' and PQQ' (Prop.3). Construct cones with same bases and vertices A and P; compare cones by compounded ratios of bases and heights (Props. 5,12) and use equality of axes to conclude cones are equal; then segments (each 3/2 cone by Prop.22) are equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 24 — paraboloid segments scale as squares of axes
rubrics_metrics.description: If two segments of a paraboloid of revolution are cut off by planes drawn in any manner, the segments are to one another as the squares of their axes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose planes through axis producing circular sections with diameters Pp and P'p' and build cones on these circles with common vertex A. Use Prop.23 to show segments equal to those with circular bases whose axes equal given axes. Since cones are in ratio (PN^2 : P'N'^2)·(AN : AN') and PN = AN, deduce segments scale as AN^2 : AN'^2. Use construction of circular sections perpendicular to axis and proportionality of cone volumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 25–26 — hyperboloid segment volume ratio formula
rubrics_metrics.description: In a hyperboloid of revolution, with vertex A and axis AD of a segment cut off by a plane, and CA the semi-diameter through A (collinear with AD), the ratio (segment) : (cone with same base and axis) = (AD + 3·CA) : (AD + 2·CA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to plane hyperbolic section BAB' with tangent HF parallel to base touching at A, and CA meeting BB' at D with CA producing bisect. Construct cylinder/frustum through the base with axis AD and a cone with vertex A. Choose a cone V so that V : (cone ABB') = HD : A'D and show by contradiction using inscribed/circumscribed stacks of cylinders/frusta and detailed rectangle/gnomon arithmetic that the segment equals V, yielding the stated ratio. The proof is long and uses arithmetic decompositions of sums of rectangles and careful comparison of parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 27–30 — spheroid segment ratio relations
rubrics_metrics.description: For a spheroid with centre C, a plane meeting the axis cuts off a segment (not greater than half) with vertex A and axis AD and remaining segment axis A'D; then (first segment) : (cone or segment of cone with same base and axis) = (CA + A'D) : A'D (equivalently expressed in terms of CA and AD). In particular, if plane passes through centre (segment is half spheroid), half the spheroid is double the cone/segment with same vertex and axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work in plane of axis with elliptic section A B A' B' and tangents parallel to base touching at A and A'; construct planes through tangents parallel to base, show they touch the spheroid at A and A' and that AA' passes through centre C and bisects BB' at D. Draw cylinder/frustum and cone with axis AD and vertex A, set up a cone V with V : (cone ABB') = HD : A'D and proceed by contradiction via inscribed/circumscribed stacks of cylinders/frusta similarly to the hyperboloid case. The detailed proof uses rectangle and gnomon decompositions and comparisons (Prop.1 and Prop.2 style) to force equality and obtain the ratio formulas.
